Return Of Part IV: Execution

Chapter 10 Preliminary draft

Risk and Sizing

Stops, the 1% rule and expectancy.

Decide how you will get out before you get in. A position's size, its stop and its target are one decision, made on paper while you are calm.

Decide the exit before the entry

Most losses that hurt are not the planned ones. They are the ones with no plan: a position drifts down, hope fills the gap, and the exit gets decided in the worst possible mood. The fix is simple. Before you place an order, write down where you will leave if you are wrong and where you will leave if you are right.

This is the return of capital principle applied to a single trade. You protect the money first, then ask what it might earn. In the Ladder, every Level 2 entry carries a written entry price, stop and target. No written exit, no trade.

The stop is where the idea is wrong

A stop is not a random percentage. It is the price at which your reason for buying no longer holds. If you bought a breakout, the stop sits where the breakout has failed. If you bought a pullback to support, it sits just below that support. Pick the level from the chart or the thesis first. Then size the position to fit it, never the other way around.

Moving a stop further away to avoid being stopped out is the same as having no stop. You may tighten a stop as a trade works. You do not loosen it.

The 1% rule and the sizing formula

The plan states the rule this way: size each position so that hitting the stop costs about 1% of the satellite. The satellite is the active slice of your money, so 1% of it is the most one idea can take from you.

The formula has three steps. Dollars at risk is 1% of the satellite. Risk per share is the entry price minus the stop price. Shares equal dollars at risk divided by risk per share. Round down to whole shares.

Notice that the position cost varies while the loss at the stop stays near $100. A wide stop means fewer shares. A tight stop means more. The risk is the constant, not the share count.

Expectancy: what a system earns per trade

Expectancy is the average result of a trade across many trades. The formula: win rate times average win, minus loss rate times average loss.

Here is arithmetic with invented inputs. Suppose a system wins 40% of the time, with an average win of $300 and an average loss of $100. Expectancy is 0.40 × $300 minus 0.60 × $100, which is $120 minus $60, or $60 per trade. The system loses more often than it wins and is still positive. Flip the numbers (win 60%, average win $100, average loss $300) and you get $60 minus $120, or a loss of $60 per trade, even though it wins most of the time.

Win rate alone tells you almost nothing. The size of wins against losses matters just as much. This is why the journal measures expectancy, and why the Ladder's promotion rule asks for it.

The risk is the constant, not the share count.

Why a string of losses is survivable

Even a good system has losing streaks. At 1% risk per trade, ten losses in a row cost a little under 10% of the satellite: 0.99 multiplied by itself ten times is about 0.904, so roughly 9.6% down. That hurts, but it leaves you in the game with a working account. The next streak of wins, sized the same way, starts from there.

Now size at 10% per trade and the same ten losses leave you with about a third of your money. The math of recovery is harsh: a 50% loss needs a 100% gain to get back. Small risk per trade keeps the hole shallow and the climb out short.

Open questions

  • What counts as the satellite's size for the 1% calculation: the starting balance, or the current balance as it changes?
  • Is 1% the right ceiling for each Level, or should it differ by strategy?
  • What is the maximum total risk across all open positions at once?
  • How do you handle a gap past the stop, where the fill is worse than the stop price?
  • How many journal trades are enough before you trust an expectancy figure?
